Joining Gavin are New World Magazine columnist Emma-Kate Symonds; Constant Méheut, The New York Times correspondent in Ukraine; Venetia Rainer, Daily Telegraph Foreign Editor and host of Iran: The Latest; and Sarah Morris, France 24’s correspondent in Spain.
summary: Catch up with the World This Week with Gavin Lee. In just 45 minutes, make sense of seven extraordinary days in global affairs, as Gavin and his handpicked panel of four leading international correspondents unpack the stories shaping the world — and the questions behind the headlines.
author: France 24

title: Alberto Núñez Feijóo seeks to keep right‑wing voters mobilised in Spanish elections
content: “His main political platform is to say, I am not Sánchez, I am the opposite of Sánchez.” As Spain heads to the polls, what do Alberto Núñez Feijóo's campaign and political career tell us about the kind of prime minister he might become? Javier Carbonell, Policy Analyst at the European Politics and Institutions Programme and lecturer at Sciences Po in Paris, joins Gavin Lee to break down the Popular Party leader's efforts to avoid the mistakes of 2023 and keep right-wing voters mobilised without galvanising the left.
summary: Alberto Núñez Feijóo’s campaign focuses on positioning himself as the opposite of Sánchez. Javier Carbonell, Policy Analyst at the European Politics and Institutions Programme and lecturer at Sciences Po in Paris, discusses Feijóo’s efforts to keep right‑wing voters mobilised while avoiding galvanising the left.
author: France 24

title: Ukraine offers Black Sea ceasefire to allow food exports, awaits Moscow reply
content: Ukraine has submitted a Black Sea ceasefire proposal aimed at restoring food exports, a senior Ukrainian official confirmed on Friday. The proposal’s details were forwarded to international allies, and Kyiv is awaiting a response from Moscow. The announcement followed a day after Russia reportedly attacked two foreign grain carriers near the port of Odesa, according to Ukrainian authorities.
summary: Ukraine made a Black Sea ceasefire offer to enable food exports and shared the details with international allies, a senior Ukrainian official said on Friday. Kyiv is waiting for a response from Moscow after Russia attacked two foreign grain carriers near Odesa the previous day, Ukrainian authorities said.
author: France 24

title: Uganda to pull troops from key town in DR Congo amid Kinshasa tensions
content:
Uganda has announced the withdrawal of its troops from a key town in North Kivu, eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. The decision follows a deterioration in relations with Kinshasa after provocative comments from Uganda’s army chief.  

In a separate health alert, pregnant women are struggling to cope with extreme heat. Health experts warn of growing risks for unborn babies, including dehydration and premature births.  

Meanwhile, many migrants in South Africa who sought safety, opportunity and a better life now face hostility, violence and growing exclusion. Anti‑immigration sentiment is gaining ground, eroding the country’s promise as a land of hope.
summary: Kampala announced the withdrawal of its troops from a key town in North Kivu, eastern DR Congo as relations with Kinshasa deteriorate after provocative comments from Uganda's army chief. Pregnant women are coping with extreme heat risks and migrants in South Africa face hostility, violence and growing exclusion.
author: France 24

title: S&P changes France outlook to negative from stable
content: Rating agency S&P revised France’s outlook to “negative” from “stable” on Friday. The downgrade was justified by growing budget pressures, as weak economic growth and higher interest costs make it harder to reduce the deficit.
summary: Rating agency S&P revised France’s outlook to negative from stable on Friday. S&P cited growing budget pressures, weak economic growth and higher interest costs as making it harder to reduce the deficit.
author: France 24

title: Albanian youth protest against political rigidity and corruption, say fewer will emigrate
content: Albanian youth have staged protests against a rigid political system and corruption, striking at the government of Prime Minister Edi Rama. The demonstrations also indicate that fewer young Albanians are choosing to emigrate in search of a better future.
summary: Youth protests against a rigid political system and corruption have shaken the government of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama. The protests also show that fewer young people are willing to emigrate in search of a better future.
author: DW World

title: Serbian media owner Dragan J. Vucicevic arrested amid scrutiny of pro‑Vucic outlets
content: The media owner of Informer TV, Dragan J. Vucicevic, has been arrested. The move has prompted questions about whether Serbia is holding the individuals behind its pro‑Vucic media outlets accountable, or whether the arrest is part of a broader political power struggle.
summary: Media owner Dragan J. Vucicevic was arrested in Serbia. The arrest has raised questions about whether Serbia is holding the people behind the pro‑Vucic media accountable or engaging in a political power struggle.
author: DW World

title: Gambia election on Dec. 5 sees President Adama Barrow seek third term
content: President Adama Barrow is seeking a third term as Gambians vote on December 5. The election will test the opposition’s appeal and the country’s progress on democratic reform.
summary: President Adama Barrow is seeking a third term as Gambians vote on December 5. The election will test the opposition’s appeal and the country’s progress on democratic reform.
author: DW World

title: Norwegian low‑cost airline Norse Atlantic files for bankruptcy amid fuel price spike
content: Norway’s low‑cost carrier Norse Atlantic, founded only a few years ago, filed for bankruptcy after a prolonged struggle to achieve profitability. The airline cited a spike in aviation fuel prices, which it attributed to the war in Iran, as the decisive factor driving the insolvency.
summary: Norse Atlantic, a low‑cost airline founded a few years ago in Norway, has filed for bankruptcy. The filing follows a spike in aviation fuel prices caused by the war in Iran, which the airline said pushed it into insolvency.
author: DW World

title: Dutch police seize 26 critically endangered turtles from traveler bound for Hong Kong
content:
Dutch authorities seized 26 Vallarta mud turtles from the luggage of a passenger bound for Hong Kong.  

The species, discovered in 2018, is critically endangered with roughly 300 individuals in the wild; nearly one‑tenth of that number were found in the luggage, bound in duct tape.
summary: Dutch authorities seized 26 critically endangered Vallarta mud turtles that were packed in duct‑tape in the luggage of a passenger traveling to Hong Kong. The tiny turtle, discovered in 2018, is thought to number about 300 in the wild, making the seized animals roughly one tenth of the total population.
author: DW World

title: EU budget summit collapses amid divisions over Ukraine funding and US tech tax
content: An EU leaders summit on the bloc’s seven‑year budget collapsed as member states could not agree on how to fund Ukraine. The draft budget also proposes a 3 % levy on U.S. technology firms, intended to raise additional revenue for the EU.
summary: An EU leaders summit on the bloc's seven-year budget fell apart amid divisions over how to fund Ukraine. The budget proposal also includes a 3% tax on US tech companies, in a bid for the EU to generate additional funds.
author: DW World

title: Canada Supreme Court largely upholds Quebec's Bill 21 secularism law
content: Canada’s Supreme Court has largely upheld Quebec’s Bill 21, the province’s law that bans public‑servants from wearing religious symbols. The government said the ban is needed to protect a secularist society, while critics contend the measure weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.
summary: The Supreme Court of Canada largely upheld Quebec's Bill 21, which bans religious symbols for public servants. The government said the law protects a secularist society, while critics say it weakens fundamental rights protections.
author: DW World

title: UNHCR warns deep funding cuts threaten protection for refugee women and girls
content: During the 16 Days of Activism, the UN Refugee Agency warned that deep funding cuts are severely weakening protection for refugee and stateless women and girls and others at risk of gender‑based violence. The agency highlighted cases such as Mariam, who survived a decade of captivity and rape by Boko Haram militants.
summary: Serious funding cuts are severely weakening protection for refugee and stateless women and girls and others at risk of gender‑based violence (GBV). The warning cites Mariam, who survived a decade of captivity and rape at the hands of Boko Haram militia.
author: UN News

title: Jared Kushner calls Russian invasion of Ukraine a misunderstanding in 70‑minute interview
content: Trump’s son-in-law and senior negotiator paints Russian invasion of Ukraine as a misunderstanding to be resolved In the space of a 70-minute interview, Jared Kushner – Donald Trump’s son-in-law and a prominent US negotiator in Russia, Gaza and Iran – probably did more to reveal why the world is mired in entrenched conflicts than a thousand geopolitical tomes or seminars. During the conversation this week with Mathias Döpfner, the chief executive of the Axel Springer media publisher, Kushner gave a rare insight into his diplomatic technique, offering a string of homilies that veered close to banalities: “You have nothing until you have something”, “diplomacy is like untying knots on a fishing line for his son”, and “you play the ball from where it lands”.
summary: Jared Kushner calls Russian invasion of Ukraine a misunderstanding in 70‑minute interview.
author: Guardian World

title: Belgium orders Google to halt southern datacentre build over refused permit
content:
Belgian authorities have ordered Google to stop construction of a large data centre in the south of the country after the firm’s request to modify the original planning permission was not approved. Inspectors reported that the building was almost finished, with structural work completed, even though the permit had been refused. Raphaël Stokis, a Wallonia regional official, told public broadcaster RTBF that the site had been visited and the work observed.

Greenpeace’s report notes that Google continued building despite the planning appeal remaining unresolved. The halt applies until the planning issues are resolved.
summary: Belgium orders Google to halt southern datacentre build over refused permit.
author: Guardian World

title: Police say criminals robbed fans at Don Toliver Manchester concert after unknown substance
content:
Police are working with agencies across Europe after similar incidents occurred at two other Don Toliver concerts. A group of organised criminals is believed to have carried out robberies during Don Toliver’s Manchester concert, where an “unknown substance” was released, police have said, with similar incidents having occurred at another two of the US rapper’s gigs in Europe.

Greater Manchester police said they were working to identify the suspects and the substance involved during the incident at the Co‑op Live Arena on Sunday evening.
summary: Police are working with agencies across Europe after similar incidents occurred at two other Don Toliver concerts. Greater Manchester police are trying to identify the suspects and the unknown substance released at the Co-op Live Arena on Sunday evening.
author: Guardian World

title: NSW Labor picks Jade Tyrrell for Lane Cove in “captain’s call” preselection
content: Exclusive: Ryde councillor Penny Pedersen was asked by Labor head office not to nominate for Lane Cove in March state election Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast Labor’s New South Wales leadership has been accused of alienating members and undermining the democratic process, after multiple state election candidates were preselected by “captain’s call” instead of the rank and file. The premier, Chris Minns, announced on Friday that commercial litigator Jade Tyrrell will be Labor’s candidate for the marginal Liberal-held seat of Lane Cove at March’s state election.
summary: NSW Labor picks Jade Tyrrell for Lane Cove in “captain’s call” preselection.
author: Guardian World

title: Victorian Labor faces wipeout, may lose 30+ seats as voters shift to Liberals, One Nation
content:
A former ALP strategist warned that the Ben Carroll‑led Labor government in Victoria could lose more than 30 seats in Saturday’s election, potentially falling behind Pauline Hanson’s One Nation party. The comment appears in a guide to the 2026 Victorian election that also offers voters information on party promises and a daily political email, app and podcast.

After 12 years in office, the Labor government is described as facing an electoral wipeout as the state heads to the polls. Campaign polling has consistently favored the Coalition, and the latest Newspoll released on Thursday placed the Coalition 15 points ahead on a two‑party‑preferred basis.
summary: A former ALP strategist says the Ben Carroll Labor government could lose more than 30 seats in Saturday’s Victorian election, falling behind Pauline Hanson’s One Nation party. The latest Newspoll released Thursday puts the Coalition 15 points ahead on a two‑party‑preferred basis as Labor faces a possible wipeout after 12 years in office.
author: Guardian World

title: Jess Wilson’s sewage plant lease risks water, wetlands and won’t cut debt, experts say
content: Academic says Victorian Liberal proposal to privatise treatment plants and generate profit with no compromise of services ‘a total furphy’ Victorian election 2026 guide: what you need to know Confused about who to vote for? Check the parties’ key promises and policies Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast Experts have warned the Victorian Liberals’ plan to lease Melbourne’s sewage treatment plants is a “smoke and mirrors” way to pay off debt that risks compromising the state’s water resources and crucial wetlands for nearly a century. On Thursday – two days out from the election – the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, announced plans for a 90-year lease of the Eastern and Western treatment plants, which process the vast majority of the city’s sewage and are run by Melbourne Water.
summary: Opposition leader Jess Wilson announced a 90-year lease of the Eastern and Western sewage treatment plants run by Melbourne Water. Experts warned the plan is a “smoke and mirrors” effort to pay off debt that could compromise water resources and wetlands and would not reduce the state’s debt.
author: Guardian World

title: Canada Supreme Court 6-1 Ruling Upholds Quebec's Bill 21 Barring Religious Symbols
content:
Canada’s top court largely upheld Quebec’s secularism law, Bill 21, which bars public sector workers from wearing conspicuous religious symbols. The 6‑1 decision was released on Friday morning and has drawn close attention for highlighting the tension between minority rights and the government’s power to override those rights.

In its ruling, the Supreme Court held that Quebec may shield Bill 21 from most court challenges on the basis that the law violates charter rights.
summary: In a 6-1 decision released on Friday morning, Canada’s Supreme Court largely upheld Quebec’s Bill 21, which bars public‑sector workers from wearing conspicuous religious symbols. The court ruled Quebec may shield the law from most court challenges.
author: Guardian World

title: ‘Abusive and insulting to Canadians’: campaign to oust US ambassador presented to parliament
content: Hundreds of thousands of Canadians call for Pete Hoekstra to be declared ‘persona non grata’ A petition signed by nearly 290,000 Canadians calling on Mark Carney’s government to oust Pete Hoekstra as US ambassador to Canada was formally presented to the House of Commons on Thursday, a sign of the strained relations between the neighboring countries. Elizabeth May, a Canadian Green party member, originally opened the petition for signatures in July 2026 after a woman from Calgary sponsored it. The petition requests that the Canadian government declare Hoekstra “persona non grata” due to his “US” diplomatic interference in Canadian domestic affairs”.
summary: ‘Abusive and insulting to Canadians’: campaign to oust US ambassador presented to parliament.
author: Guardian World

title: Astronomers capture red giant merger AT2025abao in Andromeda galaxy
content:
Astronomers have documented a rare stellar merger in the Andromeda galaxy, designated AT2025abao, involving a red giant star nicknamed "Big Bao" and its smaller companion, "Little Bao." The event began when researchers detected a bright flash in a region of the galaxy where such explosions were not expected. Investigating the cause, the team identified a slow, continuous brightening over two years that traced back to a star, known as WNTR23bzdiq / WTP19aalzlk, which had been steadily increasing in brightness since 2019 after a period of stability lasting 30 years. This star was identified as a red giant, a phase in stellar evolution where a star expands significantly after exhausting the hydrogen in its core.

The team theorized that Big Bao, which has a mass seven times that of the sun and is 350 times larger, expanded rapidly and violently, swallowing its smaller companion. Little Bao subsequently spiraled into Big Bao’s core in fewer than 10 orbits. This process was monitored by a variety of ground- and space-based telescopes, including NASA’s NEOWISE, SPHEREx, and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), as well as the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii. The culmination of the event occurred in October 2025, when a massive eruption was observed by the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) and the Wide-field INfrared Transient ExploreR (WINTER) at Caltech’s Palomar Observatory.

Data from SPHEREx in July 2025 indicated that prior to the eruption, Big Bao was fading in optical light while brightening in infrared. This suggested the star was cooling and emitting dense clouds of gas and dust that enveloped it. When Little Bao collided with Big Bao’s core, stellar material was ejected at speeds of approximately 1.8 million miles per hour. This ejected matter struck the previously emitted envelope of gas and dust, producing the flash of light recorded on October 17, 2025.

Further analysis was conducted using data from the James Webb Space Telescope, which measured the total mass of dust and gas around Big Bao two months before the eruption. These measurements allowed the team to determine that Little Bao had a mass of about 70% of the sun’s mass. Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University, a team member, noted that the luck of having detailed observations for several years prior to the merger provided an unprecedented glimpse into the conditions leading to such cosmic events.

The research, which highlights the collaborative effort of multi-facility and multi-team astronomical discoveries, was published in the journal Nature on November 18. Karambelkar described the completion of the data analysis as the closure of one chapter in a broader story, emphasizing the significance of the coordinated observations in understanding the violent collision.
summary: Astronomers observed a red giant star named Big Bao devour its smaller companion, Little Bao, resulting in a massive eruption in the Andromeda galaxy detected in October 2025. The event was tracked by multiple telescopes, including JWST and NEOWISE, and the findings were published in Nature.
author: Space.com

title: Netflix's 'In a Holidaze' Features Maddie Ziegler, Dennis Quaid
content:
Maddie Ziegler and Dennis Quaid discuss the appeal of low-budget holiday films, which have evolved into a modern festive tradition. Ziegler, who gained fame on Dance Moms and later worked with Sia and in West Side Story, stars in In a Holidaze, a new Netflix original scheduled to release on 2 December. Speaking from Los Angeles, the 24-year-old performer noted that audiences seek escapism in the current state of the world. She described the project as a new experience, as she had never previously acted in a romantic comedy, but expressed enthusiasm for the role given her lifelong love of Christmas movies.

In In a Holidaze, Ziegler portrays Maelyn, a restless young woman trapped in a holiday time-loop at her family’s cabin. The character must relive the same Christmas repeatedly until she learns to trust her instincts and pursue happiness. The film is characterized as a "fuzzy" and "sugary-sweet" production that aligns with Netflix’s typical Christmas offerings. These streamer originals generally focus on romance and family dynamics, employing an aesthetic and ironic tone comparable to Hallmark Channel films, which are widely associated with clichéd holiday storytelling.
summary: Maddie Ziegler and Dennis Quaid star in Netflix's new holiday film 'In a Holidaze', which premieres on December 2. Ziegler plays Maelyn, a restless twenty‑something who relives the same Christmas at her family's cabin until she learns to trust her gut and take chances on what makes her happy.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Tomlin calls Steelers 'dumpster fire' as Brady rips Rodgers
content:
Mike Tomlin, who coached Aaron Rodgers and the Steelers last year, described the quarterback’s recent exit from Pittsburgh as a “dumpster fire” during a Thanksgiving broadcast. Speaking at half-time of the Kansas City Chiefs-Buffalo Bills game on NBC, Tomlin stated that he was upset by the situation, noting that he has presided over similar incidents in his 19 years of coaching. He added that he believes “Steeler Nation” is also upset about the developments.

Tom Brady, a longtime peer of Rodgers, also weighed in on the drama. The source notes that Rodgers was released after a diatribe involving McCarthy, and Tomlin remarked that the quarterback was “beloved” by his teammates. Both figures commented on the event on Thursday, with Tomlin expressing his personal frustration over the circumstances surrounding Rodgers’s departure.
summary: Mike Tomlin described the Pittsburgh Steelers as a dumpster fire following Aaron Rodgers' dramatic exit from the team. Tom Brady also weighed in on the situation, criticizing Rodgers for breaking locker room sanctity.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Magnus Carlsen to play in record 800-player XTX Markets Super Rapid in London
content:
Magnus Carlsen will headline the XTX Markets Super Rapid at the London Classic, attracting a record field of 800 competitors. Organisers raised the venue capacity at the London Novotel West in Hammersmith from 500 to 800 for the 5‑6 December event, making it the largest single‑tournament ever staged on English soil, though it remains second to Germany’s Grenke Open at Karlsruhe internationally.

The world No 1 is making a very rare appearance in an open tournament. In the first round he is expected to be paired with an opponent rated in the low 1800s. Full details of the Super Rapid and how to enter are available through the event’s official channels.

Meanwhile, Gukesh and Sindarov are set to battle in Geneva, adding another high‑profile match to the month’s chess calendar.
summary: World No. 1 Magnus Carlsen will compete in the XTX Markets Super Rapid at the London Classic, which has expanded its field to 800 players. The tournament will be held at the Novotel West in Hammersmith on 5‑6 December, and Carlsen is expected to face an opponent rated in the low 1800s in round one.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Dončić’s Lakers lead NBA with 15‑3 record, neck‑and‑neck in MVP race
content:
The Los Angeles Lakers have entered the 2024‑25 season with a dramatic roster overhaul that included the trade of Luka Dončić from the Dallas Mavericks. The move, which many observers feared could interrupt Dončić’s ascent to superstar status, has instead coincided with the Slovenian guard playing at an MVP level. The Lakers’ early record—15‑3—places them at the top of the NBA standings, ahead of the Spurs and the 76ers, who both sit at 15‑4.

Dončić’s trade was controversial because he had just finished a run to the NBA Finals with Dallas and was viewed as a key piece in a team built around his strengths. Critics worried that relocating him to a franchise that did not fit his skill set could stall his prime. However, the current season’s results suggest that the Lakers’ new chemistry is effective, with Dončić matching the production of other league leaders.

The MVP race is now a tight contest between Dončić and Victor Wembanyama. While the San Antonio Spurs and their French superstar were considered title and MVP favorites before the season, the Lakers and Dončić are keeping pace in every statistical category. The upcoming NBA Cup matchup on Friday night will pit the Lakers’ 15‑3 record against the Spurs’ 15‑4, creating a rare high‑stakes regular‑season duel between the league’s top records and leading MVP candidates.
summary: After a trade from the Dallas Mavericks, Luka Dončić is playing at an MVP level for the Los Angeles Lakers. The Lakers have the best record in the NBA at 15‑3 and Dončić is neck‑and‑neck with Victor Wembanyama in the MVP race.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Liam Delap’s struggles are symbolic of damaging Chelsea churn
content:
The constant turnover of players and staff has made consistency an elusive quality at Stamford Bridge. Liam Delap arrived at Chelsea in the summer of 2025 and was praised by Enzo Maresca as the next Harry Kane. A year later, however, he had no chance of joining Kane in England’s World Cup squad.

Delap’s form at the club was described as miserable. The only bright spot was that Chelsea made a profit when they sold him to Nottingham Forest for £50 million last summer. His single season at Stamford Bridge included one serious hamstring injury, one league goal, one red card and little else.

Analysts at other clubs rated him at Ipswich and argued that Chelsea was the wrong fit for his direct style of play. The article concludes that the real mistake was the decision to sign him in the first place, rather than the choice not to give him another season.
summary: The constant turnover of players and staff has made consistency an elusive quality at Stamford Bridge Liam Delap came and went. He joined Chelsea in the summer of 2025 and was hailed by Enzo Maresca as the next Harry Kane.
author: Guardian Sport

title: England's heavy schedule counters All Blacks' 'no gas' narrative before rematch
content: Figures indicate England’s players have far more rugby miles in their legs than Saturday’s opponents but Borthwick has managed to balance heavy schedule The prevailing narrative emerging before England’s rematch with New Zealand on Saturday is that the All Blacks are running on fumes. The forwards coach, Jason Ryan, has said that “there is not much juice in the tank” while Graham Henry, who led them to the 2011 World Cup title, has continued the theme in even starker terms. “It’s the end of the season and we’re buggered. They’ve just got no gas in the tank.” It is understood that narrative has raised a number of eyebrows within the England camp. The view, as England seek to clinch a third straight win over New Zealand for the first time in the history of the fixture, is best summed up as, “welcome to our world”. We are nearing the end of a gruelling year for the All Blacks, who give the impression they cannot wait for their season to end, but the grind in England, that which led to Maro Itoje being ordered to take the summer off, is at the very least comparable.
summary: England's heavy schedule counters All Blacks' 'no gas' narrative before rematch.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Macron condemns Marseille violence; Fernandes misses Manchester United training
content:
The article offers a concise preview of the football season’s upcoming weekend. It highlights key fixtures, league tables, and a list of “ten things to look out for” in the Premier League. The piece also notes that readers can access an infographic detailing these points.

A quiz element is included to engage fans. The writer shares that they answered the first seven questions correctly before faltering, likening the experience to the performance of Manchester City. This anecdote sets the tone for the interactive segment.

The quiz question posed asks which player is the second‑top scorer in the Premier League over the last 12 months, with Erling Haaland identified as the top scorer. No further details or answers are provided in the source.
summary: Macron condemned the violence in Marseille. Fernandes missed a Manchester United training session.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Jamie Overton's Five-Wicket Haul Turns the Gabba Script, England Beats Australia
content:
The Gabbatoir, the nickname for the Gabba in Brisbane, has long been known for delivering “ritual guttings” to visiting English cricket teams. Traditionally, England’s sides have left the ground in disarray, battered on the field and still echoing with boundary‑side abuse.  

On a muggy Friday night at Vulture Street, that script was reversed. Jamie Overton’s fiery five‑wicket haul powered England to a decisive win in the second match of the series, giving the tourists a 2‑1 lead with two games still to play.
summary: Jamie Overton took a fiery five-wicket haul to lead England to a win over Australia at the Gabba. The win flipped the traditional Gabba script, giving England a 2-1 lead with two matches remaining.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Man City owners must be forced to sell, say Premier League clubs
content: Senior figures at several Premier League clubs have told BBC Sport that Manchester City’s owners should be forced to sell the club as a punishment for breaching financial rules. The clubs’ representatives argue that the sale would address the regulatory violations.
summary: Senior figures at some Premier League clubs say Manchester City's owners must be forced to sell the club. They argue this should be a punishment for breaking financial rules.
author: BBC Sport

title: Bayern Munich's Jamal Musiala faces lifelong medical condition, uncertain return
content: Bayern Munich’s Jamal Musiala may never return to his previous level and will have to manage a medical condition for life. The next steps for him remain uncertain.
summary: Jamal Musiala of Bayern Munich may never return to his previous level. He will have to manage a medical condition for the rest of his life.
author: BBC Sport

title: Trump and NATO Secretary‑General Rutte Urge Russia to Stop Expanding War in Ukraine
content: President Trump and NATO Secretary‑General Mark Rutte urged Russia not to expand its war with Ukraine. The call followed a meeting Wednesday at Mar‑a‑Lago in Florida, after peace talks had made little headway in recent weeks. The two leaders released a joint statement.
summary: President Trump and NATO Secretary‑General Mark Rutte urged Russia not to expand its war with Ukraine. They released a joint statement after a meeting at Trump’s Mar‑a‑Lago resort in Florida.

title: America is back at war, and Americans are still at the mall
content: Retired Marine Corps Lieutenant Colonel Kevin M. Schmiegel calls for local communities to move beyond symbolic gestures such as Veterans Day parades. He urges the creation of actionable plans that support service members and their families, emphasizing employment opportunities, mentorship, and integration to help them thrive.
summary: Retired Marine Corps Lieutenant Colonel Kevin M. Schmiegel says local communities should move beyond symbolic Veterans Day parades. He calls for actionable plans that provide employment, mentorship, and integration to help service members and their families thrive.
author: The Hill

title: Nate Silver Says Trump Could Be Removed from Office After Midterm Turmoil
content: Polling analyst Nate Silver stated on the “Still Counting” podcast that there is an “absolutely” chance President Trump could be removed from office following midterm backlash against the GOP and his administration. During the episode, Silver engaged with co-hosts Galen Druke and Clare Malone in a discussion regarding this potential outcome.
summary: Polling analyst Nate Silver said there is an "absolutely" chance that President Trump could be removed from office after backlash during the midterms. He made the statement on the "Still Counting" podcast with co-hosts Galen Druke and Clare Malone.
author: The Hill

title: Bad weather disrupts Thanksgiving, Trump calls for GDP probe
content:
Severe weather is upending Thanksgiving plans across the country, with travelers preparing for flight delays and cancellations as a powerful nor’easter moves up the East Coast. The storm has already pushed back the annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday and prompted emergency declarations in New York and New Jersey.

President Trump demanded action on Thursday, though the specific request is not detailed in the update.
summary: Severe weather is upending Thanksgiving plans across the country, causing flight delays, cancellations, and pushing the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday. President Trump called for a probe into GDP data.
author: The Hill

title: Lutnick Faces Pressure as Senators Target AI Chip Leaks to China
content:
Senators from both parties have placed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick in the hot seat after revelations that Nvidia sold billions of dollars’ worth of high‑tech chips to a Singapore‑based company. That company’s former senior executive, Alice Huang, is accused of being a Chinese spy.  

Lawmakers in both parties criticized President Trump’s intervention in the matter.
summary: Senators in both parties say Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is in the hot seat after Nvidia sold billions of dollars’ worth of high‑tech chips to a Singapore‑based company linked to alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang. Lawmakers criticized President Trump’s intervention in the matter.
author: The Hill

title: Trump’s Influence Shapes 2028 Presidential Election Landscape
content: The 2028 presidential election cycle is dominated by Donald Trump, whose influence over potential successors JD Vance and Marco Rubio continues to shape a highly unpredictable political landscape. Trump's presence remains a central factor as the race unfolds.
summary: Donald Trump continues to influence potential 2028 presidential candidates JD Vance and Marco Rubio. His influence shapes a highly unpredictable political landscape.
author: The Hill

title: Trump's Immigration Changes Nearly End Asylum; Supreme Court to Review
content: Trump’s sweeping immigration changes—including an asylum ban, mass firings, and new legal maneuvers—have effectively ended asylum. Advocates now look to the Supreme Court, which will soon hear whether these shifts deny people due process.
summary: Trump's sweeping immigration changes — an asylum ban, mass firings and new legal maneuvers — have all but ended asylum. The high court will soon consider whether some shifts deny people due process.
author: NPR Politics

title: UK net migration drops to 77,000, a “big moment” according to ONS
content: "Big moment" as net migration falls to tens of thousands. BBC political editor Chris Mason explains the significance of migration in the UK falling to 77,000, according to the Office for National Statistics.
summary: Net migration in the UK fell to 77,000, according to the Office for National Statistics. BBC political editor Chris Mason called the decline a “big moment” and explained its significance.
author: BBC Politics

title: Britons’ cow’s milk sales at record low as many opt for plant-based
content:
Official data shows Britons are buying less cow’s milk than at any point since records began. Guardian analysis of the government’s family food survey indicates the average person bought 1.8 pints (1,024 ml) of cow’s milk a week in 2024/25, the lowest level in the record’s 52‑year history.  

That amount is less than half the milk purchased in 1974.  

The decline is attributed to environmental and animal welfare concerns and taste preferences, which have driven the rising popularity of alternatives, including plant‑based options.
summary: Environmental and animal welfare concerns, as well as taste preferences, behind rising popularity of alternatives Has milk gotta lotta bottle? It may not have as much as it used to, with official data showing Britons are buying less cow’s milk than at any point since records began.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Aged Care Move Disrupts Long-Standing Doctor Relationships, Experts Urge Better Handover
content:
Moving into residential aged care can disrupt long‑standing relationships with doctors and other health‑care providers.  

Experts say this highlights the need for stronger handover processes to protect continuity of care for older Australians.

title: UT Southwestern Finds Cellular Brake That May Explain Excessive Myelin Growth
content: UT Southwestern Medical Center researchers identified a cellular “brake” that prevents excessive myelin growth in the brain. This brake may be linked to mental health conditions such as major depressive disorder, anxiety, and post‑traumatic stress disorder.
summary: UT Southwestern Medical Center researchers identified a cellular 'brake' that prevents excessive myelin growth in the brain. The brake may hold clues to mental health disorders such as major depressive disorder, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Puberty's Hormone Swings and Their Impact on Teenage Girls' Mental Health
content: The article explores how puberty’s wild hormone swings impact teenage girls’ mental health. It notes that the stereotype of a moody teenager masks a more complex reality, involving fluctuating hormones, emotional swings, and a brain undergoing major renovations.
summary: The article explains that the stereotype of a moody teenager masks a complex reality of fluctuating hormones, emotional swings, and brain renovations. It examines how puberty's hormone swings affect teenage girls' mental health.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Ebola Data Suggest Loperamide May Benefit Patients in West Africa
content: An international research team has, for the first time, systematically evaluated the use of the antidiarrheal drug loperamide in patients with Ebola virus disease. The study focuses on patients in resource‑limited settings who receive loperamide during the early stages of illness, when oral intake is still possible. Ebola virus disease commonly causes severe diarrhea and vomiting in the majority of affected patients.
summary: Ebola virus disease causes severe diarrhea and vomiting in most patients. An international research team has systematically evaluated the potential benefit of giving loperamide early in the illness for the first time.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Northeastern Researchers Struggle to Get Newborns to Sleep During Brain Scans
content:
Newborns are notoriously hard to soothe, a fact that every parent knows.  
At Northeastern University, researchers face an added obstacle: getting these tiny subjects to sleep while they undergo a brain scan.
summary: Northeastern University researchers face the challenge of getting newborns to sleep during brain scans. The difficulty mirrors what many new parents experience when trying to get a newborn to sleep.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Signatures stay recognizable when written with the non-dominant hand
content: A study shows that a signature can stay recognizable when written with the non‑dominant hand, even though different muscles are used. This suggests an internal pattern for the action that can be reused in varied circumstances. Researchers ask whether this pattern develops only after years of practice or can aid learning from the outset.
summary: A signature can remain recognizable when written with the non-dominant hand, even though different muscles produce it. This suggests an internal pattern for the action that can be reused in different circumstances.
author: Medical Xpress

title: RNA therapy proposed to treat heart damage in Fabry disease
content: Fabry disease, also called Morbus Fabry, is an inherited metabolic disorder in which certain fatty substances are not broken down sufficiently, leading to their accumulation in various organs and causing serious damage. An RNA‑based therapy is being explored as a potential approach to treat heart damage associated with this condition.
summary: An RNA therapy approach is being explored to treat heart damage in Fabry disease. Fabry disease is an inherited metabolic disorder in which certain fatty substances cannot be broken down sufficiently, leading to accumulation and serious organ damage.
author: Medical Xpress

title: England health officials urge at‑risk groups to vaccinate amid surge in severe flu cases
content: Health officials in England report a recent surge in severe flu cases. In response, they are urging individuals who are most at risk to receive a flu vaccination as soon as possible.
summary: A surge in severe flu cases has been observed. Health officials in England have urged those most at risk to get vaccinated as soon as possible.

title: Nonlinear optical lattice boosts spatial coherence by concentrating light in a single mode
content: Light waves exhibit varying degrees of coherence, defined by the consistency of phase relationships across space or time. A nonlinear optical lattice enhances spatial coherence by concentrating light into a single mode. These reliable methods for improving light coherence may facilitate the development of high-quality lasers and scientific instruments.
summary: A nonlinear optical lattice increases spatial coherence by concentrating light into a single mode. This improvement could enable the development of high‑quality lasers and scientific instruments.

title: New soil test could help farmers avoid costly crop damage
content: Herbicides are essential for weed control, yet residual chemicals in the soil can damage crops planted in later seasons, especially during dry conditions. A new soil test aims to help farmers avoid this costly crop damage.
summary: Herbicides are essential for controlling weeds. However, chemicals left in the soil after application can damage crops planted in subsequent seasons, especially during dry conditions.

title: Caltech study uses cosmology math to characterize ocean flows
content:
A new study from Caltech applies a mathematical framework borrowed from cosmology to ocean data, enabling researchers to analyze and characterize individual flow features amid the churning chaos of the sea.

Using this technique, the team can measure and describe features in maps of the ocean surface, distinguishing ocean flows that appear identical when examined with conventional analysis tools.
summary: A new Caltech study applies a mathematical framework from cosmology to analyze ocean data and characterize individual flow features. The technique allows researchers to differentiate ocean flows that appear identical when using standard analysis tools.

content: A paper presented at the IEEE Technology and Engineering Management Society Conference (TEMSCON LATAM) in Quito, Ecuador, in June 2026, offers a common statistical approach for tracking changes in attention and forecast errors separately. The study highlights the distinction between attention and surprise, noting its relevance for public-interest forecasts that guide media planning and traffic capacity decisions.

title: Newly observed particles in quantum simulator hint at third particle class
content: A recent experiment using a quantum simulator has detected particles that have not been seen before. The findings provide evidence that a third class of particles, beyond the long‑established categories of bosons and fermions, may exist.

title: New Scientist Book Club reads Kit Chapman's The Age of Alchemy
content: The New Scientist Book Club is reading The Age of Alchemy in December “ A handful of lime and another of sulfur in fine powder. Place them in a vessel containing strong vinegar or the urine of a small child. Heat it from below, until the liquid appears like blood. Advertisement Decant this properly, and use. ” Unknown, Leiden Papyrus X, c. 300 CE In 1827, amid the dark, silent balm of an Egyptian night, a graverobber pulled a treasure from the sands. At first, the raider was frustrated; scavenging the tombs near Thebes, he had hoped to uncover a priceless heirloom, or a nugget of gold that would sparkle with lustre in the starlight. Instead, he had found only a clutch of rolled scrolls, made of papyrus and sealed against the elements. For a moment, he considered casting the documents aside and leaving them for the desert. Then greed got the better of him. Westerners loved all things Egyptian, he reasoned. Since the French had arrived with Napoleon, the new field of “Egyptology” had swept the continent, capturing the imagination of scholars and the wealthy. It was almost as popular as the new science of “chemistry”. Surely, if he took his find to the market, he’d find some gullible fool willing to buy it. The buyer’s name was Jean d’Anastasy, and he was anything but a fool. Born in Greece as the son of a Damascus merchant who had won and lost his fortune in the Napoleonic Wars, d’Anastasy had used his family’s connections to set himself up as a grain merchant in Alexandria, before scheming his way into being named the local Consul General for Sweden and Norway. Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter When d’Anastasy wasn’t trading – or rescuing enslaved girls during the Greek War of Independence against the Ottoman Empire – he ran a side-hustle, “procuring” relics from Ancient Egypt and selling them to the salons of Europe: statues to the British Museum in London; rings and jewels to the Louvre in Paris; even a pair of sphinxes that still sit on the banks of the Neva River in St Petersburg. He quickly saw the value of the papers, paid for them, and shipped them back to Europe. Some went to Stockholm, and some to Leiden University in the Netherlands. Among the Leiden trove was one of the most remarkable finds in history: a papyrus scroll with a list of recipes, each with crystal-clear instructions written in Greek. While we have damaged cuneiform tablets and later copies of older works, the Leiden Papyrus X, written around 300 CE, is the oldest surviving alchemy book in history. It is a guide for Egyptian artisans to create wondrous riches, seemingly out of nothing. There are methods on how to polish silverware, cheap alternatives for making knock-off purple robes, and how to create gold lettering by mixing saffron and tortoise bile. These are all real instructions, and all recipes that work (even if, today, there are cheaper ways to get the same result). Among them is the greatest secret in alchemy. It’s called the “invention of sulfur water” and is the recipe at the start of this chapter. Sulfur and lime (calcium oxide, not the fruit) are gardening supplies that you can buy in a hardware store, and if you don’t have a small child that needs a wee to hand, strong vinegar from the supermarket will work just as well. While you shouldn’t try this at home, the result, after you heat the mix for an hour, is a red-brown goop and a kitchen that reeks of rotten eggs. These are calcium polysulfides, making up lime sulfur. It’s a nasty substance – an alkali that can cause skin irritation and even blindness if you get it in your eyes. Today, we use this for pest control, but in ancient times it was how you created gold. Well, the appearance of gold. Once you’ve got your “sulfur water”, any metal object submersed – a coin, nail or paperclip – will gain a thin, yellowy film coating. The Leiden Papyrus X isn’t just the oldest alchemy book in history. It’s a tried-and-tested guide for tricksters. We may not know who wrote the document, but we do know that if you had walked into the author’s workshop 1,700 years ago, you’d have been swindled. Or that’s how it seems. The truth, as we’ll learn, is that something else was going on that’s even more fascinating. But we’re getting ahead of ourselves. The 28 best popular science books of 2026 From space-time to saunas, here are the very best popular science books published this year that you should be adding to your Christmas list The Leiden Papyrus X isn’t what most people think of when they picture alchemy. We think of it as a pseudoscience, a blend of religious beliefs, ancient superstition and gilded dreams, with only the occasional glimpse of something that might work underneath. If you subscribe to the traditional view, this is the best you can hope for when it comes to studying any chemistry earlier than about 1650. Before the Enlightenment, there were only wizards, witches and wishful thinking. Then suddenly, whoosh, in a flash of gunpowder, a crackle of electricity and bubbling fizz from a test tube, a new science arrived to change our world. This book turns that idea on its head. No one person created chemistry, and even if they had, it certainly wouldn’t have been some white European in a powdered wig. Chemistry didn’t appear overnight and there is no one moment when it came into existence. It was a gradual transformation that built on millennia of knowledge. Choosing to ignore chemistry during the Age of Alchemy does a disservice to thousands of men and women, across the world, who guided us from the first campfire to the modern age. This book is divided into three parts. In the first, we look at how early chemistry worked, from the Stone Age up to the emergence of alchemy, and how it set the basic principles for what alchemy, and later chemistry, would become. In the second, we go on a trip around the world. Practically every history of alchemy just focuses on the western traditions – mainly because they are the best studied. But we’re going to look at what was happening with chemistry in the Islamic world, China, the Indian subcontinent and even the Americas. Some of this is alchemy, and some of it isn’t, but it all plays a role in the tapestry of science. Finally, the third section returns to Europe, where we’ll look at how alchemy changed (or, to use the alchemical term, transmuted), over the course of several hundred years, into the science we know today. My journey has led to travels across six continents and taken me on adventures through deserts and jungles, tombs and tomes, and some of our most fabled cities. I have explored old roads and met the researchers busy paving new ones. The result is a story that is both a mirror to progress and a love letter to science, one that offers a glimpse into the past and shows how it all connects to our daily lives, often in surprising and roundabout ways. Chemistry is everywhere and is linked to everything. It is painfully human. It is filled with our mistakes, beliefs and hubris. It showcases our noble endeavours, destructive potential and indomitable spirit. And it allows us to appreciate how science, whether through petty rivalries, oppression and colonisation, or religious fervour, has always been political. © Kit Chapman This is an extract from The Age of Alchemy by Kit Chapman, the December read for the New Scientist Book Club. Sign up for the club here, and join the discussion on Discord here. When you make a purchase via the links on this page, we receive a commission.
summary: The New Scientist Book Club is reading The Age of Alchemy by Kit Chapman in December. The book argues that chemistry developed gradually over millennia rather than emerging suddenly in Europe.

title: New Scientist Book Club: How urine changed the course of human history
content:
The New Scientist Book Club has selected The Age of Alchemy by Kit Chapman as its December read, featuring an exploration of urine’s historical significance. The accompanying article argues that urine was a transformative substance in human history, serving as a foundational chemical agent for various civilizational developments. While science progresses through a complex interweaving of ideas rather than a linear sequence, the text identifies urine as a key ingredient in this historical tapestry, noting that alchemists’ failed quest for the Philosopher’s Stone overlooked the practical value of this common biological fluid.

The development of early civilization relied heavily on chemistry, with fire providing warmth and cooking capabilities while urine contributed to leatherwork. Urine contains urea, which bacteria break down into ammonia, a base that softens organic matter and tans hides. This process was essential for survival across the Americas, Europe, Africa, and Asia, supporting the production of clothes, structures, and commercial goods even in cultures that did not develop a bronze age, such as the Aztec and Sub-Saharan African societies.

In ancient Rome, urine was valued for its use in laundries to whiten togas, leading Emperor Vespasian to levy a tax on draining urinals. When his son complained about the tax, Vespasian responded with the phrase pecunia non olet, meaning money does not stink. A portion of the revenue generated from this tax was used to construct the Colosseum, a structure now recognized as one of the wonders of the world. The utility of urine also extended to early chemical knowledge in Alexandria, Egypt, where artisanal trade secrets known as cheimeia included recipes for faking gold using polysulfides. One such recipe, found in the Leiden Papyrus X, suggested using the urine of a small child, although modern understanding indicates that water is a more effective alternative for the chemical reaction.

By the 17th century, urine became a critical component in the gunpowder industry. Saltpetre, or potassium nitrate, was a key ingredient in this weapon, which originated in Chinese herbal medicine. To produce saltpetre, manure heaps were mixed with potash and mortar and moistened with urine to extract nitrates. This method was employed from Europe to Japan and persisted until the 19th century; during the US Civil War, the Confederacy utilized urine to maintain its ammunition supply.

The most significant scientific contribution attributed to urine occurred in 1669 in Hamburg, where alchemist Hennig Brand isolated phosphorus. Brand had been searching for the philosopher’s stone using 1,500 gallons of fermented urine collected in his basement. The concentrated urine in his experiment began to glow, revealing the first chemical element discovered in modern times. Although Brand initially kept the discovery secret, he eventually sold the recipe to a friend, allowing the finding to be shared globally. Today, urine remains important in medicine as a source of biomarkers for diagnostic tests and was the original source of drugs such as human chorionic gonadotropin and follicle-stimulating hormone for fertility treatment.
summary: A detail from Joseph Wright’s 1771 painting The Alchemist Discovering Phosphorus, showing Henning Brand in 1669 Science History Images/Alamy Imagine you could boil the development of science down to a single ingredient. A magical, mystical compound that transformed human history.
author: New Scientist

title: Engineering antibiotics could expand the pool of new drug candidates
content:
MIT researchers have devised a dual‑strategy approach that could broaden the range of viable antibiotics by addressing the safety issues that have previously ruled out many potent antimicrobial agents. The team, led by MIT Research Scientist Tahoura Samad and senior author Sangeeta Bhatia, published their findings in Nature Communications and focused on calicheamicin, a highly toxic drug originally used in cancer therapy.

Calicheamicin, isolated from Micromonospora echinospora, kills cells by damaging DNA. Although it has been approved for treating acute myeloid leukemia, its toxicity led to its removal from the market and later re‑approval at lower doses. To repurpose the compound as an antibiotic, the researchers attached it to an albumin‑binding domain, a small protein that circulates in the bloodstream. The drug is linked via a cleavable bond that is only broken by neutrophil elastase, an enzyme produced by immune cells that accumulate at infection sites. When the conjugate reaches a bacterial infection, the linker is cleaved and the drug is released to kill bacteria.

Despite the targeted delivery, the conjugated drug still caused significant liver damage in mice. To mitigate this, the team engineered an “antidote” protein, CalU19, derived from the bacterium that naturally produces calicheamicin. CalU19 was fused to albumin so it could circulate in the bloodstream and neutralize any drug that escaped the infection site, acting as a “security guard” that protects organs such as the liver.

In mouse models of bacterial pneumonia caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus, the drug‑antidote combination cleared infections while preventing liver damage. The researchers also demonstrated the conjugate’s activity against laboratory strains of methicillin‑resistant S. aureus, E. coli, and Klebsiella pneumoniae. They are now exploring antidotes for other drug candidates, including antibiotics that are limited by kidney toxicity, and suggest the strategy could be applied to existing cancer drugs to reduce side effects.

The study was supported by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, the Virginia and D. K. Ludwig Fund for Cancer Research, the National Cancer Institute, the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences, the Koch Institute’s Marble Center for Cancer Nanomedicine, Joel and Meredith Gantcher, and a postdoctoral fellowship from the Ludwig Center at the Koch Institute.
summary: As more strains of dangerous bacteria become resistant to existing antibiotics, the quest to find new drugs has become more urgent. In hopes of expanding the pool of antibiotic candidates, MIT researchers have found a way to significantly improve the safety profile of drugs with antimicrobial activity that had previously been discarded.
author: MIT News

title: Reduced oxygen breathing triples lifespan of mice with motor neuron degeneration
content:
Oxygen is essential for life, but too much can become dangerously toxic, especially in people with certain neurological and mitochondrial disorders.  

Scientists at Gladstone Institutes discovered that defective proteins can disrupt the ability of mitochondria to consume oxygen, allowing harmful levels to accumulate in tissues.  

Remarkably, mice with a genetic disorder that causes motor neuron degeneration lived three times longer when they breathed air containing less oxygen.
summary: Scientists at Gladstone Institutes found that defective proteins can impair mitochondrial oxygen consumption, causing harmful oxygen buildup. Mice with a genetic disorder causing motor neuron degeneration lived three times longer when breathing air with reduced oxygen.

title: Giant horned mammals may have had fewer sexual differences than thought
content: Scientists have long believed that giant horned mammals that appeared soon after the dinosaurs’ extinction displayed pronounced sexual dimorphism. New research suggests males and females may have differed less than previously thought, challenging a classic example of sexual dimorphism. The findings also prompt reevaluation of how historical biases may have influenced interpretations of extinct species.
summary: Giant horned mammals that appeared shortly after the dinosaurs died out may have had far fewer physical differences between males and females than scientists once believed. This discovery challenges a classic example of sexual dimorphism and raises questions about historical biases in interpreting extinct animals.
author: Science Daily

title: Urolithin A supplement boosts brain blood flow during memory task in obese adults
content:
A naturally derived dietary supplement called urolithin A is reported to potentially help the brain obtain more oxygen and nutrients when needed.  

In a randomized clinical trial of 50 middle‑aged adults with obesity, participants took the supplement daily for four weeks. Researchers observed increased blood flow to the brain during a challenging memory task, with the effect most pronounced in a region associated with working memory.
summary: In a randomized clinical trial of 50 middle‑aged adults with obesity, participants took the naturally derived supplement urolithin A daily for four weeks. The supplement increased blood flow to the brain during a challenging memory task, especially in a region linked to working memory.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists identify infancy and early school years as high‑risk periods for screen time
content: Scientists say that children may be most vulnerable to screen time during two developmental windows: infancy and the beginning of formal schooling. Their research links higher screen exposure in these periods to lower academic achievement and weaker working‑memory performance in later years.
summary: Scientists have identified infancy and the start of formal schooling as two critical periods when screen time may be especially detrimental to children's learning and memory. Greater screen exposure during these developmental windows was linked to poorer academic performance and weaker working memory years later.
author: Science Daily

title: Virginia Tech scientists turn PVC into high‑performance engine oil in three hours
content: Virginia Tech scientists have developed a process that converts discarded polyvinyl chloride (PVC)—one of the world’s hardest-to-recycle plastics—into a component for high‑performance engine oil. The method transforms the waste into a lubricating material in three hours, offering a potential route to repurpose plastic pollution and make lubricant production more sustainable.
summary: Virginia Tech scientists have developed a process that converts discarded PVC into a lubricant material for high‑performance engine oil in three hours. The breakthrough could turn a major source of plastic pollution into a valuable industrial resource and make lubricant production more sustainable.

title: Exercise-released fat-burning molecule boosts muscle strength, reduces fatigue
content:
Researchers discovered that a naturally occurring molecule released during exercise helps muscles become stronger, resist fatigue, and withstand damage.  

The molecule is already available as a dietary supplement and could open new avenues for treating muscle deterioration associated with type 2 diabetes.
summary: Researchers discovered that a naturally occurring molecule released during exercise helps muscles become stronger, resist fatigue, and withstand damage. The molecule, already available as a dietary supplement, could open new avenues for treating muscle deterioration associated with type 2 diabetes.

title: Scientists find two opposite microscopic spirals inside narwhal tusk
content: The narwhal’s iconic spiral tusk—historically prized in Europe as a unicorn’s horn—has been shown to embody a striking natural engineering feature. Advanced X‑ray imaging by an international team of scientists revealed that the tusk houses two microscopic spirals intertwined and twisting in opposite directions.

content: Harvard‑led researchers have developed a microscopic device that generates 120 times more ultraviolet light than previous comparable approaches by efficiently converting red light into UV. The breakthrough could unlock smaller quantum computers, ultra‑precise atomic clocks, and compact environmental sensors.

title: Landsat 9 captures cloud‑shrouded Shivelyuch volcano amid ongoing eruptions
content:
Shivelyuch, also known as Shiveluch, is a volcano on Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula that is noted for frequent eruptions and persistent cloud cover. A recent image from the Operational Land Imager (OLI) aboard Landsat 9, taken on November 8 2026, shows the snowy peak obscured by clouds that hover beneath its 3,283‑meter (10,771‑foot) summit. The clouds do not blanket the volcano’s caldera or its northern upper slopes, leaving a clear view of those areas.

The volcano’s upper reaches contain a caldera that measures 9 kilometers (5.6 miles) across and opens to the south. Within the caldera a dark lava dome is visible, formed by vents that extrude viscous magma. Lava domes at Shivelyuch undergo cycles of growth and collapse, and when they collapse they can trigger fast‑moving avalanches of hot ash and rock known as pyroclastic flows.

According to the Kamchatka Volcanic Eruption Response Team (KVERT), effusive eruptions of lava and explosive activity had been occurring at Shivelyuch for months as of November 2026. Satellites routinely detect thermal anomalies from the volcano, and on the day the image was captured KVERT reported a plume of resuspended ash drifting 120 kilometers (75 miles) eastward. This level of activity is described as relatively tame for the mountain.

Explosive eruptions from Shivelyuch periodically loft ash several kilometers into the atmosphere, allowing it to travel great distances and pose risks to aircraft. In July 2026, an ash plume rode the jet stream over the Bering Sea into Alaskan airspace, prompting the cancellation of multiple flights, according to news reports.

The Earth Observatory image was produced by Lauren Dauphin using Landsat data from the U. S. Geological Survey, and the accompanying story was written by Lindsey Doermann. The image and story are part of NASA Earth Observatory’s “Image of the Day” series.
summary: Landsat 9 captures cloud‑shrouded Shivelyuch volcano amid ongoing eruptions.

content: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 27 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos!
