title: Coalition to privatise Melbourne sewage plants and sell state land and renewables if it wins election
content:
The Liberal and Nationals’ pre‑election policy costings, released by opposition leader Jess Wilson on Thursday, outline a plan for a Victorian Coalition government. If elected, the coalition would privatise two sewage plants and sell state‑owned land, renewable energy assets, and the “air rights” between Richmond train station and the Melbourne Cricket Ground.

Wilson issued the costings just two days before the state election, after more than 1.5 million Victorians had already cast their ballots. The documents present the parties’ key promises and policy details ahead of the vote.
summary: Coalition to privatise Melbourne sewage plants and sell state land and renewables if it wins election.

title: Labor inquiry says new defence laws could have significant human rights impact
content:
A Labor‑chaired inquiry warned that new defence legislation granting officials the authority to use lethal force against suspected trespassers in designated zones could have “significant” human‑rights implications. The committee highlighted the absence of requirements to provide detained individuals with fresh drinking water or humane conditions, and cautioned that the broad changes might affect members of the public who inadvertently enter a defence security zone that has not been publicised.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese defended the laws, describing criticism of them as “nonsense” and “conspiracy theories” from the far left and far right.
summary: Labor inquiry says new defence laws could have significant human rights impact.

title: Senate inquiry says Labor's Support at Home program leaves older Australians without care
content: The Support at Home system has ‘baffling’ bureaucracy and ‘rations and denies care’, says Greens chair of Senate inquiry Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast Many older Australians are dying before they can access home support, paying exorbitant fees, and being pushed into hospitals and residential care before they are ready because of a flawed federal government aged care program, a Senate inquiry has found. The inquiry is examining the impact of the Support at Home program, which launched in November 2025 and has been plagued by complaints of making care harder to access and more expensive. The inquiry was due to finish in November, but has been extended for a further year after receiving almost 300 submissions.
summary: The Senate inquiry found that the federal Support at Home program, launched in November 2025, is plagued by “baffling” bureaucracy, high fees and delays that leave many older Australians dying before receiving care. The inquiry, chaired by the Greens senator, has been extended for a year after receiving almost 300 submissions.

title: Wife of Japanese journalist Yuki Imai pleads for his release after Russia detains him
content:
The wife of Japanese journalist Yuki Imai has issued an emotional appeal for his release after he has been detained in Russia for more than a month on suspicion of spying. Imai, a reporter for the Hokkaido Shimbun, was arrested in mid‑October while preparing to return to Japan from a two‑year assignment at the newspaper’s bureau in Yuzhno‑Sakhalinsk on Sakhalin Island.

Imai is being held in Moscow on allegations that he conducted “espionage” while working for the newspaper in Russia’s far east. The wife’s plea highlights her distress and her request that the authorities reconsider his detention.
summary: Yuki Imai, a reporter for the Hokkaido Shimbun, was arrested in mid‑October in Moscow on suspicion of espionage while preparing to return to Japan from a two‑year assignment in Yuzhno‑Sakhalinsk, Sakhalin. His wife has issued an emotional appeal asking for his release after more than a month of detention.
author: Guardian World

title: China says it may take necessary measures after Trump proposes 20% tariff
content: Beijing says new levies amount to ‘political manipulation’, while Brazil ‘will not yield to this type of threat’ Trump proposing new tariffs on 14 partners including China and EU Beijing has said it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” after Donald Trump’s administration proposed new tariffs on goods from China and other major trading partners, triggering a global backlash. Among the suggested levies on 14 major trading partners announced on Wednesday, China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. It would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.
summary: China says it may take necessary measures after Trump proposes 20% tariff.

title: Bob Woodward's memoir 'Secrets' details his career and the craft of investigative reporting
content: The journalist who helped bring down Nixon on false starts, Watergate, and the art of cultivating a source ‘I have always disliked the term ‘investigative reporter’.” So writes Bob Woodward, one of the most celebrated reporters of our time – the man whose Watergate reporting with Carl Bernstein undoubtedly changed the US presidency and journalism itself for ever. His longtime boss, the Washington Post editor Ben Bradlee, disliked the term too: “All reporting is investigative,” Bradlee would say. The term conjures a certain sophistication, perhaps, but part of the beauty of a reporter’s work is how deceptively unsophisticated it can be. Secrets is a far-ranging, revealing memoir of an extraordinary career, but more than that, it is an ode to grinding it out – knocking on doors, asking and asking again, listening, taking notes, making notes on the notes, patiently following every lead to exhaustion. In a media ecosystem saturated with fast and flimsy takes, this feels like a tonic. The real star of his story, Woodward seems to insist, is the shoe leather.
summary: Bob Woodward's memoir 'Secrets' is a far-ranging account of his extraordinary career, including his Watergate reporting with Carl Bernstein. The book emphasizes the deceptively unsophisticated nature of reporting, focusing on persistence and following leads.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Review: Jon Fosse's Vaim Hotel sequel explores surreal captivity in new novel
content:
Jon Fosse’s 2025 novel, Vaim Hotel, serves as the second volume in a loosely connected trilogy set in the fictional Norwegian town of Vaim. The book is a sequel to Vaim and explores the experience of a man who is stripped of the elements that define his identity. Translated by Damion Searls, the narrative is written in Fosse’s characteristic hypnotically recursive style, consisting of a single sentence.

The story begins with a man in his 50s who drives to Vaim for reasons he cannot fully articulate. He decides to stay at the empty Vaim Hotel, unaware that he may never leave. The novel features Brita, the hotel owner, a mysterious female figure before whom the male protagonist’s agency fails. This dynamic mirrors the themes of the predecessor, where a man encounters a woman he secretly loved in his youth. In that earlier volume, the woman requests to move with him to their hometown on a boat named after her, despite being married.

The predecessor, Vaim, also depicts a man who has died, with the woman returning to her husband and demanding he answer to a specific name and move into the home of the man she had previously left him for. The husband describes these events as strange and chooses that word for his tombstone. Reviewers note that both books feature a sense of powerlessness in the men and a dream-like, surreal randomness to the events.

Fosse’s narrative choices in Vaim Hotel are described as thwarting easy rationalization. The work is characterized as Beckettian in its appreciation for the absurd and the tediously mundane. It is presented as a tale of captivity that is only slightly less disorienting than its predecessor, owing to the thematic connections between the two volumes.
summary: Jon Fosse's new novel Vaim Hotel is the second volume in a trilogy set in the fictional Norwegian town of Vaim. The book features a man who lodges at the empty Vaim Hotel under the influence of its owner, Brita, in a story described as a tale of captivity.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Photographer Niall McDiarmid captures vibrant colors to counter muted world
content: Photographer Niall McDiarmid seeks out vivid colours, such as bright green kebab shops and red stockings, to counteract what he describes as a muted beige and monochrome world. The accompanying visual feature highlights these vibrant scenes as antidotes to everyday dullness.
summary: Photographer Niall McDiarmid seeks out bright colors, such as green kebab shops and red stockings, to provide an antidote to the world's muted beige and monochrome tones.

title: Andy Taylor, Duran Duran guitarist, dies at 65
content:
Andy Taylor, the guitarist for the 1980s pop band Duran Duran, has died at the age of 65.

He was diagnosed with stage four metastatic prostate cancer in 2018, and publicly disclosed the diagnosis in 2022 as the band approached induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

Taylor’s career was marked by significant chart success during the 1980s.
summary: Andy Taylor, the guitarist for 1980s pop band Duran Duran, died at age 65. He had been diagnosed with stage four metastatic prostate cancer in 2018 and publicly disclosed the diagnosis in 2022 as the band approached their Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction.

content: The County Tyrone town was shortlisted as one of 15 possible locations for the inaugural UK Town of Culture 2028, with the chance to win £3m.
summary: Strabane, a town in County Tyrone, was shortlisted as one of 15 possible locations for the inaugural UK Town of Culture 2028, with a chance to win £3 million. The bid was later withdrawn after it caused great division.

title: Aaron Rodgers accuses Steelers coach Mike McCarthy of misconduct in ESPN interview
content: From a half-time huddle gone wrong to an ultimatum over play-calling, here’s what the quarterback said Wednesday in a scorched-earth appearance on Pat McAfee’s show Barely 12 hours after the Pittsburgh Steelers announced that Aaron Rodgers would be deactivated and Mason Rudolph would start Friday’s game against the Denver Broncos, the four-time NFL Most Valuable Player left no bridge unburned in a surprise call-in to ESPN’s The Pat McAfee Show. In a 34-minute appearance on Wednesday afternoon where he spoke uninterrupted for long stretches, Rodgers accused Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy of falling asleep in a quarterback meeting, skipping walkthroughs and falling behind on film study. He also said the 63-year-old McCarthy broke a half-time huddle against Philadelphia with the words “One, two, three, Packers”. According to Rodgers, McCarthy denied falling asleep at the team facility.
summary: Aaron Rodgers appeared on ESPN's The Pat McAfee Show to criticize Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy's preparation and play-calling. Rodgers alleged that McCarthy fell asleep in a meeting and used incorrect team names during a half-time huddle.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Alejandro Garnacho left out of Aston Villa plans despite Unai Emery's interest
content:
Unai Emery has reportedly left out Alejandro Garnacho from Aston Villa’s plans, a decision that mirrors the treatment of Harvey Elliott last season despite the club’s ongoing attacking struggles. This week marks three years since Garnacho scored for Manchester United in a 3-3 Champions League draw against Galatasaray in Istanbul. At that time, the winger was a teenage star and a regular starter, having recently won the Premier League’s goal-of-the-season award for an overhead kick at Goodison Park.

During that period, Garnacho was central to Manchester United’s future, sharing the pitch with Victor Lindelöf and Aaron Wan-Bissaka, who are now his teammates at Aston Villa. He continued to perform well, scoring twice in a 3-2 victory against Villa on Boxing Day and again in a win over West Ham, which led to a memorable celebration with Kobbie Mainoo and Rasmus Højlund. Garnacho concluded that season by scoring against Manchester City at Wembley in the FA Cup final, cementing his status as a beacon of hope for the club alongside Mainoo.
summary: Unai Emery wanted the winger, but Alejandro Garnacho has been left out in the cold at Aston Villa despite the club's attacking struggles. The article notes this situation is similar to Harvey Elliott's experience at the club last season.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Gukesh and Sindarov draw Game 2 of world chess championship in 20 moves
content:
India’s Gukesh Dommaraju and Uzbekistan’s Javokhir Sindarov drew the second game of their world chess championship match on Wednesday at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in the Geneva suburbs. The encounter concluded in just 20 moves and 1 hour 57 minutes, ending by threefold repetition. This result leaves the overall match score level at 1–all.

The game was notably brief, marking one of the shortest classical world title games since the reunification of rival championships in 2006. It was also the first game to finish in under two hours since Ding Liren and Ian Nepomniachtchi drew their 11th game in just over 100 minutes in Astana in 2023.

In this encounter, World champion Gukesh opened with the London System. The next game is scheduled for Thursday, with Sindarov set to play with the white pieces.
summary: India’s Gukesh Dommaraju and Uzbekistan’s Javokhir Sindarov drew the second game of their world chess championship match in 20 moves, leaving the score level at 1-all. Sindarov will play with white in Game 3 on Thursday at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in the Geneva suburbs.

content: Liverpool defeated Club Brugge in a clinical Champions League match, bouncing back from a previous defeat. Alexander Isak scored twice, with Florian Wirtz also finding the net to secure the victory for the hosts.

content: A Fulton County, Ga., judge on Wednesday paused her own order requiring the county to provide copies of ballots seized by the FBI earlier this year to the Georgia State Election Board. Superior Court Judge Kelly Lee Ellerbe suspended the directive, which she had issued Tuesday, after county election officials filed a notice of appeal.

content: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) will miss the postponed Macy’s Thanksgiving parade on Saturday due to scheduled surgery on his right leg. The mayor confirmed at a Wednesday press conference that he is undergoing the procedure on Friday after tearing his Achilles tendon. Mamdani stated he was “very disappointed” to be unable to attend the rescheduled event.
summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani will miss the postponed Macy’s Thanksgiving parade because he is scheduled to have right‑leg Achilles tendon surgery on Friday. He confirmed at a Wednesday press conference that he could not attend the rescheduled event and expressed disappointment.

title: Rod Simms argues Australia should tax gas industry to boost revenue
content:
Rod Simms argues that increasing tax revenue from Australia’s gas industry is a straightforward public policy measure. He notes that fossil fuel companies currently do not pay for the natural resources their businesses rely on. Simms contends that while there are calls for the government to return the budget to surplus, achieving this through large expenditure cuts is difficult due to rising costs associated with an ageing population and defence spending.

Simms suggests that successfully balancing the budget requires focusing on the revenue side alongside expenditure control. He identifies collecting more tax from the gas industry as the easiest step to address ongoing budget deficits, which are forecast to continue well into the future.
summary: Rod Simms states that fossil fuel companies are effectively not paying for the natural resources their businesses depend on. He contends that collecting more tax from the gas industry is the easiest step to help address continuing budget deficits.

title: How to prepare youth to respond to firearm injury risk
content: Firearm injury is the leading cause of death for adolescents in the United States. While research indicates that most firearm owners prioritize safety, current prevention strategies for youth have largely focused on policy change rather than teaching adolescents how to identify injury risk.
summary: Firearm injury is the leading cause of death for adolescents in the United States. Most firearm owners prioritize safety, research shows, but strategies aimed at firearm injury prevention among youth have largely focused on policy change instead of teaching them how to identify injury risk.

title: Nearly half of Hungarian children exposed to screens by 18 months
content:
Nearly half of Hungarian children are exposed to screens daily by the age of 18 months.  

What they need most for development, however, is play, physical activity, face‑to‑face interactions and active exploration of their surroundings.  

Early and intensive use of digital devices may pose risks not only because of the time spent in front of screens, but also because it can take time away from these essential experiences.
summary: Nearly half of Hungarian children are exposed to screens daily by 18 months. Early and intensive digital device use may take time away from play, physical activity, face‑to‑face interactions and exploration.

title: Culturally relevant nutrition interventions can engage Black adults more effectively
content: A recent study published in the Journal of Nutrition Education and Behavior examined ways to better engage Black adults with hypertension in digital nutrition interventions aimed at improving dietary habits and reducing cardiovascular risk.
summary: A recent study in the Journal of Nutrition Education and Behavior explored how researchers can better engage Black adults with hypertension in digital nutrition interventions. The interventions aim to improve dietary habits and reduce cardiovascular risk.

title: Ecuadorian Plant Piper carpunya Reduces Clostridium perfringens in Risotto
content:
A plant long used by Indigenous communities in Ecuador may help control bacteria in ready‑to‑eat foods.  
A study in the journal Foods found that extracts of Piper carpunya, locally called guaviduca, reduced the presence of Clostridium perfringens in a refrigerated risotto model.
summary: A study in the journal Foods found that extracts of the Ecuadorian plant Piper carpunya, locally known as guaviduca, reduced the presence of Clostridium perfringens in a refrigerated risotto model. The plant is traditionally used by Indigenous communities in Ecuador.

title: Half of adults in long COVID study report difficulty breathing 4 years later
content: A recent long‑COVID study found that 50 % of adults reported symptoms indicative of dysfunctional breathing more than four years after their initial infection. Participants with persistent breathing problems were generally younger, more often female, and had a lower likelihood of having been hospitalized during their acute COVID episode.
summary: Half of adults in a new long COVID study reported symptoms that suggested dysfunctional breathing more than four years after their initial infection. Those with persistent breathing problems tended to be younger and female, and they were less likely to be hospitalized during acute COVID infection.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Multidisciplinary intervention improves fatigue for lymphoma survivors
content: A recent study published online on November 20 in the Journal of Clinical Oncology reports that a multidisciplinary intervention can improve fatigue in lymphoma survivors who continue to experience persistent fatigue. The study found that the improvement in fatigue was sustained for up to six months after the intervention.
summary: A study published online Nov. 20 in the Journal of Clinical Oncology found that a multidisciplinary intervention improves fatigue in lymphoma survivors with persistent fatigue. The improvement was maintained for six months.

title: U.S. Age-Adjusted Stroke Death Rate Decreases 2000-2024
content:
Research published in the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report found that from 2000 to 2024 the age‑adjusted stroke death rate in the United States fell.  

However, the study noted that rates increased among certain groups during the most recent trend periods.

title: Bank of England says UK food inflation may reach 5% next year
content:
The Bank of England has warned that food price inflation in the UK could reach 5 % next year.  The forecast is driven by mounting cost pressures, an energy price‑cap rise and a possible impact from El Niño, according to the bank’s latest assessment.

The bank noted that, although food inflation is expected to accelerate, it has risen less sharply than feared since the onset of the Iran war.  This suggests that the current trajectory is more moderate than earlier projections.

Deputy governor Clare Lombardelli told MPs on the cross‑party Treasury Select Committee that food price inflation is coming in under what the bank had expected and even under what the industry had anticipated.
summary: Bank of England says UK food inflation may reach 5% next year.

content: Associate professor Petr Sulc and his research team have developed a programmable DNA-based building system. This innovation could open new possibilities for nanorobots, three-dimensional electronics, and next-generation nanotechnology.
summary: Associate professor Petr Sulc and his research team have developed a programmable DNA-based building system that could open new possibilities for nanorobots, three-dimensional electronics and next-generation nanotechnology.

title: Neolithic Denmark: Fermented Milk Held Ritual Power in Tombs
content: Experimental archaeology has examined the substances fermented in Neolithic Scandinavian pottery that were deposited in tombs. The findings suggest that fermented dairy products held symbolic significance in prehistoric funerary rituals.
summary: Experimental archaeology indicates that fermented dairy products were deposited in Neolithic Scandinavian tombs. This suggests these substances held symbolic significance in prehistoric funerary rituals.

title: Archaeologists find evidence of hunter‑gatherers in Ireland 13,500 years ago
content: A team of archaeologists and scientists has uncovered evidence suggesting Late Upper Paleolithic hunter-gatherers may have lived in southern Ireland around 13,500 years ago. This discovery potentially pushes the confirmed timeline of human arrival in the region back by nearly a millennium.
summary: A team of archaeologists and scientists uncovered evidence that Late Upper Paleolithic hunter‑gatherers may have lived in southern Ireland around 13,500 years ago. This would place human presence in the region nearly a millennium earlier than currently confirmed.

title: Sweden tops global media freedom support rankings
content: A new index has ranked Sweden as the world’s leading supporter of international media freedom. The same study notes a decline in funding from 30 major donor countries, even as threats to independent journalism continue to rise.

title: Study finds dislike of AI doesn't reduce its impact on decisions
content: New research from City St George’s, University of London shows that an aversion to artificial intelligence does not reduce its influence on people and their decision‑making. The study indicates that even those who dislike AI remain affected by the technology in their choices.
summary: New research from City St George's, University of London finds that an aversion to artificial intelligence does not lessen its influence on people. The study says AI continues to affect decision‑making even among those who dislike it.

title: Meat-Eating Dinosaurs Likely Sawed Meat with Backward-Dragging Teeth, Experiments Show
content: New experiments suggest that meat‑eating dinosaurs likely fed by dragging their teeth backward through flesh, much like a saw, rather than biting straight down like a dagger. The study proposes that this tearing motion was a key feature of their feeding behavior.
summary: New experiments suggest that meat-eating dinosaurs fed by dragging their teeth backward through flesh like a saw. This contrasts with the idea that they bit straight down like a dagger.

title: Anthropic mathematician claims to solve generalized Riemann hypothesis with Claude
content:
Mathematics is facing an existential crisis.  

On November 20, 2026, a mathematician at the AI company Anthropic claimed that while working with the model Claude, he had solved the generalized Riemann hypothesis, the most famous problem in mathematics.  

The hypothesis has remained unsolved for 167 years, and solving it could easily warrant a Fields Medal—considered equivalent to a Nobel Prize, but for mathematics.
summary: On Nov. 20, 2026, a mathematician at Anthropic claimed to have solved the generalized Riemann hypothesis while working with the model Claude. The problem had remained unsolved for 167 years and solving it could earn a Fields Medal, the mathematics equivalent of a Nobel Prize.
author: Phys.org

title: Questioning the Claim That We Know More About Space Than the Ocean
content: New discoveries about the world are made daily, from a species of deep‑sea fish to a new galaxy. A common saying claims we know more about space than the ocean, but this assertion is debated. The question hinges on how “knowing” is measured—whether by the quantity of direct observations or by the resolution of those observations.
summary: New discoveries are made daily about the world, including a species of deep‑sea fish and a new galaxy. The statement "We know more about space than the ocean" is questioned, and the criteria for determining knowledge—direct observation versus resolution—are discussed.

title: MIT and UCSB physicists find Einstein's particle motion theory incomplete for quarks
content: MIT and UC Santa Barbara physicists have found that Einstein’s classic theory of particle motion does not fully account for behavior of particles moving near light speed. Their calculations show that heavy quarks traversing an ultra‑hot plasma receive rare, unusually powerful jolts that the traditional model cannot explain.
summary: MIT and UCSB physicists find Einstein's particle motion theory incomplete for quarks.

title: Astronomers discover Phoebe, a primordial black hole only three times the Moon's mass
content:
Astronomers may have discovered a black hole born before first stars. Object named Phoebe was detected when it briefly magnified a distant star.  

Phoebe could be a primordial black hole formed just after the Big Bang. Its estimated mass is only three times that of the Moon, and it may be a 13‑billion‑year‑old relic that offers new clues to dark matter.
summary: Astronomers detected Phoebe when it briefly magnified a distant star, suggesting it could be a primordial black hole formed after the Big Bang. The object has an estimated mass only three times that of the Moon and may be a 13‑billion‑year‑old relic that could provide clues to dark matter.

title: Researchers find drug boosts energy expenditure without activating brown fat
content: Researchers have found that a drug can markedly raise the body’s energy expenditure without clearly activating calorie‑burning brown fat. This unexpected result highlights a new obstacle in developing obesity treatments that rely on the body’s natural fat‑burning mechanisms.
summary: Researchers discovered a drug that significantly increases the body's energy expenditure. The finding presents a challenge for developing obesity treatments that harness the body's natural fat-burning machinery.

title: World’s largest trial of robotic knee replacement shows no pain or mobility benefit
content:
A landmark clinical trial, the largest of its kind, evaluated robot‑assisted knee replacement surgery. The study highlighted the technology’s potential for greater surgical precision.  

Despite this advantage, the trial found that, after one year, patients showed no meaningful improvements in pain, mobility, or recovery compared with conventional knee replacement surgery.
summary: The trial found no meaningful improvements in pain, mobility, or recovery after one year compared with conventional surgery. Robot-assisted knee replacement offers greater surgical precision.

title: Scientists find brine‑pool lakes over a mile below Red Sea
content: Scientists have identified rare underwater lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea. The brine pools, described as extremely salty and oxygen‑free, are teeming with microbial life. Researchers say these environments may reveal secrets about Earth’s ancient oceans and the possibility of alien life, challenging current ideas of where organisms can survive.
summary: Scientists have discovered rare underwater lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea. The lakes, known as brine pools, are extremely salty, oxygen‑free and host microbial life, offering clues about ancient oceans and potential alien life.

title: Ask HN Feed Starved by Decline in Text Posts; Separate Ranking Proposed
content:
A Hacker News user has identified the cause behind the recent scarcity of posts on the /ask page, which had prompted community discussions about missing pagination and low post counts. The issue stems from the traditional method of selecting Ask HN stories, which were drawn from the top 1,500 ranked submissions used to generate the front page. According to the user, the proportion of text-based submissions within this top tier has declined significantly, effectively starving the Ask HN feed of new content.

To resolve this, the proposed solution is to calculate a separate list of ranked Ask HN posts rather than relying on the general front page ranking. The user clarified that while "Ask HN" is the conventional name for these entries, the category includes any post submitted without a linked URL, regardless of whether the title begins with "Tell HN" or another prefix. This post has received 87 points and 38 comments.
summary: The /ask page was running dry of Ask HN posts because the top 1500 ranked submissions list had a low percentage of text posts. The proposed solution is to compute a separate list of ranked Ask HNs.
author: Hacker News

title: 1Password breach exposes customer names and emails, not passwords
content:
1Password reported that a hacker stole customer names and email addresses after gaining access to its backend systems. The breach did not expose passwords or other information stored in customer vaults, but it could increase users’ risk of phishing attacks.

The company began investigating the incident on November 19 after an attacker accessed an employee’s corporate GitHub account. Using the compromised account, the hacker retrieved 1Password’s source code and pushed malicious code to backend services to download customer data. The number of affected users remains unknown.
summary: A hacker accessed 1Password's backend systems and stole customer names and email addresses, but did not obtain passwords or vault data. The breach began after an attacker compromised an employee's GitHub account and injected malicious code into backend services.
author: The Verge

title: EPA reports ‘zero’ airborne lead following controlled Army detonation in Iowa
content:
EPA reports “zero” airborne lead following a controlled Army detonation in Iowa.  

On November 25, 2026, the U.S. Army detonated more than 9,700 pounds of highly‑volatile, degraded lead azide on the grounds of the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa. The detonation was carried out to prevent a possible spontaneous explosion of a stockpile of material used in igniters and blasting caps. Video footage showed plumes of smoke several hundred feet high drifting south before quickly dissipating.

After the blast, the Army confirmed that all barrels at the plant were destroyed and that no secondary explosions or infrastructure damage occurred. “I believe, absolutely, that we reduced, as close to zero as it's absolutely humanly poss …” the Army spokesperson said.
summary: EPA reports ‘zero’ airborne lead following controlled Army detonation in Iowa.
author: The Verge

title: WhatsApp Adds Scheduled Messaging Feature for Private and Group Chats
content: WhatsApp's 3 billion users are getting an option that Meta says is one of the most requested features, with the ability to schedule messages in advance for both private conversations and group chats. Most messaging platforms have had this for a very long time, but now it's on WhatsApp too. If you think of a text at an inconvenient time or don't want to forget to fire off a birthday message at 4AM, you can draft it and set it to send anywhere from 10 minutes to two weeks later. The feature works with photos and videos, too. Meta: To schedule a message, press and hold the send button and pick the date and time you want it to arrive. It …
summary: WhatsApp now lets its 3 billion users schedule messages for private and group chats up to two weeks in advance. The feature, described by Meta as highly requested, works with text, photos, and videos and is accessed by holding the send button to set a date and time.
author: The Verge

title: Google’s My Channel patent seeks AI‑generated video feeds based on user data
content:
Google filed a patent last year for a system called My Channel that is designed to create feeds of personalized, AI‑generated videos and advertisements based on information the company knows about its users. The patent was rejected, but Google may appeal or resubmit an amended version, potentially bringing the concept to market.

The patent was first spotted by Patentlyze. It was filed last May and published last week. It describes using a person's demographic data and viewing history to create prompts that are fed into a large language model to generate AI videos tailored to that user.
summary: Google filed a patent for My Channel, a system that would create personalized AI‑generated video feeds and ads using users' demographic data and viewing history. The patent was rejected, but Google may appeal or resubmit, which could bring the system to market.
author: The Verge

title: Amazon ordered to recall over 400,000 hazardous products after court ruling
content:
Amazon has been ordered to recall more than 400,000 hazardous products after a court decision in its favor of the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC). The U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland ruled that Amazon is a distributor of goods, not merely a logistics provider, and therefore must carry out recalls of third‑party items.  

Amazon filed suit against the CPSC in March 2025 following the agency’s directive to recall over 400,000 “Fulfilled by Amazon” products that pose a substantial product hazard. The recalled items include faulty carbon monoxide detectors, hair dryers lacking electrocution protection, and child products.
summary: Amazon ordered to recall over 400,000 hazardous products after court ruling.
author: The Verge

title: Google Familiar Faces AI adds support for Walmart’s $35 Onn Outdoor Camera
content:
Google has added its Familiar Faces AI detection to two Walmart‑branded cameras. The $35 Onn Outdoor Camera Plug‑In and the $77 Onn Floodlight Camera Hardwired now support the feature through a Google Home update, though users must have a Google Home Premium subscription to enable it.  

Both Onn models, along with Google’s Nest Cam Outdoor (wired, 2nd gen), also receive a new remote control in the Google Home app that lets users start or stop a 30‑second security siren while viewing the live video feed. Earlier this month, Google announced Gemini Live.
summary: A Google Home update adds Familiar Faces support to Walmart’s $35 Onn Outdoor Camera Plug‑In and $77 Onn Floodlight Camera Hardwired. Access to the feature still requires a Google Home Premium subscription, and both cameras now include a remote control in the Google Home app to trigger a 30‑second security siren while viewing live video.
author: The Verge

title: Physicist Suvrat Raju tests AI on unpublished problem, plans benchmark
content:
A professor of theoretical physics at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, Suvrat Raju, recently tested a frontier artificial‑intelligence model by giving it a physics problem he had already solved but not published. Because the problem had never appeared online, Raju intended to see whether the model could answer a question it could not have simply memorized.

The AI’s response was incorrect, yet it performed better than Raju had anticipated. The unexpected level of competence led him to consider repeating the experiment in a more formal way. Together with a colleague, Raju is now working to develop a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate AI systems on theoretical‑physics problems that have not been previously documented online.
summary: Suvrat Raju, a professor of theoretical physics at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, asked a frontier AI model to solve a physics problem he had already solved but not published. The model answered incorrectly but better than expected, prompting Raju and a colleague to create a theoretical physics benchmark for AI.
author: Ars Technica

title: Kagi launches privacy‑focused Gmail rival Kagi Mail with calendar
content:
Kagi, a small software company based in Palo Alto, California, has expanded its subscription‑based search engine offering by launching a Gmail‑like email service called Kagi Mail. The service is positioned with the same emphasis on privacy, personal data sovereignty, customization and user control that Kagi promotes for its search product. Alongside the email platform, Kagi is also introducing a calendar feature, both of which are currently available only through web interfaces.

The email interface, which is in public beta, is described as minimalist and keyboard‑command driven, providing a private, ad‑free experience. Kagi Mail includes unlimited aliases and domains, an anti‑lock‑in policy for user data, 50 GB of storage, rule‑based filtering with Sieve, an MCP server, and several optional AI tools that are off by default—such as an agent for searching email history, large‑scale re‑labeling, and creating additional filtering rules. Native Android and iOS apps are slated for release in the fourth quarter of next year.
summary: Kagi, a Palo Alto subscription‑based search engine company, has introduced Kagi Mail, a Gmail‑like service that emphasizes privacy, data sovereignty and customization. The web‑only public beta provides 50 GB storage, unlimited aliases, a calendar, rule‑based filtering and optional AI features, with native Android and iOS apps planned for the fourth quarter of next year.
author: Ars Technica
